newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine bankers try conjuring trick on peso.
newsitem.headline: Philippine bankers try conjuring trick on peso.

text.p: When Philippine currency traders return to their dealing rooms next week it will be as though Friday's dramatic plunge in the peso never happened.
In theory, the peso should resume trading on Monday around 29 to 29.50 to the dollar, traders said.

That is close to the last prices before trading was suspended on Friday morning shortly after the Central Bank announced it would relax controls on the currency, leading to a de facto devaluation of 11.5 percent.
But when traders return to their dealing rooms on Monday they will find a very different rate on their screens -- the one before the peso plunged.

The reason is that the Bankers' Association of the Philippines (BAP), which controls currency trading among local banks, operates a volatility band rule which has been in abeyance for the past two years as the peso has barely moved against the dollar.

The rule, imposed by the bankers group in 1994, forces a temporary halt to trading if the peso moves above or below a 1.5 percent reference rate, which is the average rate of deals before trades were suspended. The suspension can be for up to two hours.
Because the band was exceeded in Friday's trading, the association is ignoring all trades outside the 1.5 percent band and insisting that the average on Monday morning will be 26.40 pesos.
Since the market wants the peso to be lower, it will breach the volatility band, trading will be suspended and the market will have to start all over again.
"This is a comedy of sorts. What the BAP has to address is the consequences of what they are doing. They are just prolonging the agony," Banco Santander treasurer Antonio Agcaoili said.
Traders said the rule is just as likely to create more chaos in the market as the peso tries to seek a market-determined level -- which the Central Bank has promised would be the case.
On Friday the Philippine central bank finally gave in to days of relentless speculation against the peso which followed last week's effective devaluation of the Thai baht.
Some bankers believe the volatility band rule will just sow confusion in the currency market as it it is inconsistent with the Central Bank's new policy.
"The problem with that is we're going to go against the pronouncements that we're allowing the currency to seek its own level," said Agcaoili.
"All people will do is sell" said a London-based trader, who admitted he was completely confused by the rule.

Philippine National Bank president Peter Favila, a BAP official, told reporters "the volatility band is what is putting orderliness in this market. The BAP deemed it is its responsibility to maintain orderliness in the market."
Bankers said the band will only encourage the growth of a parallel market, which would draw most of the dollars from market.
"The first deal (on Monday) is going to be a de facto suspension of trades," another said. "It is going to trade beyond the band."
Traders said they only wish the recess could be shortened so the peso would eventually go to its market-determined level.
"I think 29/29.50 is a good level to sell," the dealer said.
Another said the peso could move in a wide band band of 28/30 pesos before stabilising at 28/29 pesos in the medium term.
-- Manila newsroom (63 2) 841-8937
